notes: The p series: same origin as plain p (PMc *p > p; Bender et al. 2003a: 4; Lee & Wang p. 407). Velarised. Distinctive velarisation is found syllable-initially before a front vowel, generally e and ɛ, occasionally i, apparently never æ (pp. 404, 415). Comparison with the other Micronesian languages puts its rise after PMc; it is especially likely before e < *a, but not every such word has it (p. 415), and Lee & Wang suggest a link with low-vowel dissimilation (p. 432).

Stated against POC *i; PMc *i is taken as POc *i unchanged. Non-final *i is 'most often reflected as a high vowel', and i is the most frequent of these (p. 417): *ŋkinit > kihnis, *pitu > it-, *sili > il, *pi(dr)i > ir.
Stated against POC *i; PMc *i is taken as POc *i unchanged. Reflected as ih in only one form; the source thinks more instances would turn up in a larger database (p. 417).

Stated against POC *i; PMc *i is taken as POc *i unchanged. Rounding assimilation before *u in the next syllable: *anitu > inut, *niu(R) > nu, but not in *pitu > it-, *pitu?u > itu/itih (pp. 417-418, 426).

Stated against POC *e; PMc *e is taken as POc *e unchanged. *e is the rarest POC vowel in the data; the only reflex of non-final *e is *mpeŋka > fak 'flying fox' (p. 419). Entered as the one attested reflex, not as the regular one.
Stated against POC *u; PMc *u is taken as POc *u unchanged. 'Most often reflected as a high vowel in KSR, most frequently u' (p. 419): *kutu > kut, *sulu > sul, *tu?u(d) > tu, *?umu > um.
Stated against POC *u; PMc *u is taken as POc *u unchanged. 'Sometimes i or ih' (p. 419): *susu > titi-, *?uluŋa > ilung, *?uma > imac, *Ruŋma(?) > iwac-.
Stated against POC *u; PMc *u is taken as POc *u unchanged. 'Sometimes i or ih' (p. 419): *mputo > fiht-, *inu(m) > nihm.
Stated against POC *o; PMc *o is taken as POc *o unchanged. 'Non-final POC *o is generally reflected as o in KSR' (p. 420): *matolu > mahtol, *mponot > fonos, *mpoŋi > fong, *tolu > tol-.
Stated against POC *o; PMc *o is taken as POc *o unchanged. 'Occasionally as oh' (p. 420): *onom > ohn-, *doŋo > lohng.
Stated against POC *o; PMc *o is taken as POc *o unchanged. 'Occasionally as a non-round mid vowel' (p. 420): *topu > tuh 'sugarcane', perhaps to avoid a homonym (p. 421).

Stated against POC *a; PMc *a is taken as POc *a unchanged. *a 'may be reflected as any of the twelve surface vowels' (p. 421), and only this choice has a stated condition: oa occurs only where the next syllable has a round vowel, though a round vowel there does not always round *a (p. 422; rounding assimilation, p. 426): *ndanu(m) > sroano-, *laŋo > loang, *napo > noa, *walu > oal-.

Stated against POC *a; PMc *a is taken as POc *a unchanged. Rounded reflexes of *a occur only before a round vowel in the next syllable (pp. 423, 426): *manu(k) > won, *ma?udi(p) > moul, *patu > yot, *waka > okah.

Stated against POC *i; PMc *i is taken as POc *i unchanged. Final vowels were deleted, after the final consonants (p. 429): *anitu > inut, *patu > yot, *kinta > kuht, *kali > kuhlkuhl. Inalienable nouns keep the stem's final vowel before a possessive suffix (*tama > tuhma-, *mata > muhta-, *?ate > acsyac-; p. 429).
